newsitem.title: USA: NYS kicks off advertising for tax amnesty program.
newsitem.headline: NYS kicks off advertising for tax amnesty program.

text.p: New York State, whose advertising campaign for its new tax amnesty program got beaten to the punch by tax preparers who started offering their help early this week, on Wednesday started its campaign.

The state's second general tax amnesty program, which begins on November 1 and ends on January 31, 1997, aims to raise $110 million of new money that it otherwise would not have collected by inspiring nonfilers to come forward.

Saying the program will help ensure all residents pay their share of taxes, Michael Urbach, state commissioner of taxation and finance, in prepared remarks explained "tax amnesty is part of the state government's goal of restoring a sense of fairness to the tax system."

The total amount the amnesty program collects could well exceed the $110 million goal as individuals and businesses who owe money that the state has had trouble collecting also are likely to take advantage of the program.
But a spokesman for the state department, Kevin Quinn, did not release any overall forecasts about how much the tax amnesty program might take in.

In its three-month tax amnesty program in 1985 to 1986, the state raised $401 million, and Quinn noted that the latest one, which is open to all invidiuals and firms with less than 500 workers, has many of the same rules.

About half of the taxpayers whom the department did not know about have continued to pay taxes since they came forward in the first amnesty program, Quinn said, explaining a large number probably stopped becaue they moved or died.

When New York announced its new tax amnesty plans, there was speculation it might have been prompted by New Jersey's success last spring. That state pulled in about $350 million from its tax amnesty program, far exceeding its $70 million target, in part due to a heavy advertizing campaign.

New York plans to spend around $3 million on newspaper, radio and television advertisements, and it has set up an Internet site for people who want information. The spokesman for the state department said it considered advertizements run by tax preparers to be helpful, noting it was mailing them information about the plan and encouraging them to contact it.
After the new tax amnesty program ends, penalities for failing to pay taxes will be raised five percent.
"Once it's over, it's over," said Urbach.
The department also beefed up enforcement by adding investigative staff and new computer programs, which can match lists of licensed professionals with tax rolls, for example.

Using the new technology this month helped the department detect a number of employers who appear to have collected witholding taxes from their workers, but not sent the money on to the state, as required by law.
The tax department is continuing its probe, which could lead to criminal charges, Urbach said.
The computer matching programs also have found individuals who file federal taxes but not state taxes, and businesses that file sales taxes but not witholding taxes, he added.
